back: Drift: gradual change from small mutations, causing seasonal epidemics and the need for yearly vaccine updates. Shift: sudden major change, often from mixing of viruses from different species, which can cause a pandemic.
1918–19 (H1N1, at least 50 million deaths), 1957 (H2N2), 1968 (H3N2), 2009 (H1N1, declared a pandemic by the WHO in June).
Droplets and aerosols from coughs, sneezes and speech, and contaminated surfaces; infectious from about a day before symptoms; crowds speed spread.
Peaks in the local winter in temperate zones (northern: Nov–Mar; southern Africa: about May–Sep); occurs all year in the tropics.
Children under five, adults over 65, pregnant women, people with chronic illness or weak immunity, and health workers.
Wild aquatic birds carry influenza A; pigs can be infected by bird and human strains and act as mixing vessels; H5N1 shows the risk of avian viruses.
(Attack rate in unvaccinated − attack rate in vaccinated) ÷ attack rate in unvaccinated × 100.

Sentinel surveillance, free annual vaccine for risk groups and children, antiviral stocks, pandemic plans and hygiene campaigns; limits: partial vaccine effectiveness and winter pressure on hospitals.
